strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: system-level efficiency (latency, memory, bandwidth) of multi-agent V2X cooperative perception for real-world deployment, rather than chasing accuracy benchmarks in isolation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), multiple fusion methods (Pyramid Fusion, F-Cooper, AttFuse, V2X-ViT, Who2com, Where2comm), and both model-level and system-level metrics.

Real-world deployment evidence: latency breakdown measured on edge platforms with ROS/TensorRT (Fig. 5), power/throughput/efficiency measurements (Table 9), and an end-to-end comparison including communication-delay modeling (Table 3).

The alignment module (KL-based heterogeneity loss and L2 spatial loss) is a sensible, quantization-specific contribution that is ablated (Table 2) and qualitatively illustrated (Figs. 3, 7, 8), showing clear benefits over naive linear quantization.
Good practical value: codebook-based message representation (0.03 MB vs 8.6 MB uncompressed) and a scaling study showing larger models fit within fixed GPU memory budgets (Fig. 6).

The paper is clearly written, well organized, and the appendix provides useful ablation studies (calibration data size, calibration steps, comparison with other PTQ methods) and honest discussion of design choices.
Reproducibility is supported by an explicit plan to open-source, building on the public HEAL/V2X-Real ecosystem.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the codebook-based message representation is closely related to CodeFilling (Hu et al., 2024), which is also the strongest baseline in Table 3; the gain over it is modest (~1.2 mAP30/50). The PTQ calibration pipeline combines established techniques (Max-min init, AdaRound-style learnable rounding, BRECQ-style block-wise reconstruction).

The headline '+9.5 mAP30 over full-precision' is somewhat misleading because the full-precision baseline without compression is penalized by simulated latency/transmission effects in the system-level protocol; the comparison against the best full-precision compressed configuration (~3.8 mAP) and against CodeFilling (~1.2 mAP) is much smaller and would be a more honest framing of the contribution.

The heterogeneity and spatial alignment losses are standard divergence/L2 objectives; the paper does not provide much theoretical or mechanistic insight into why these particular forms are optimal for the fusion stage versus alternatives.
Only INT4/INT8 settings are explored; the justification for excluding 2-bit quantization is reasonable, but a broader bit-width sweep would strengthen the claim of 'fully quantized' generality.

The paper acknowledges (Section 5, Appendix B) that attention-based architectures like V2X-ViT degrade significantly under aggressive quantization and that the alignment module does not fully resolve this; this limits the generality of the proposed recipe.

System-level evaluation relies on a modeled communication latency formula (with a uniform asynchronous delay), rather than end-to-end measurements under real V2X network conditions, which slightly weakens the real-world deployment claim.

The scaling study (Fig. 6) uses only a single backbone family (PointPillar) and one GPU memory range; the claim that quantization 'unlocks' larger models is demonstrated but not thoroughly stress-tested.

Some of the performance gains may stem from the interaction of quantization with specific datasets (e.g., V2X-Real) rather than from quantization per se; cross-dataset generalization of the alignment module is not fully isolated.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely important and underexplored problem: the system-level deployability (latency, bandwidth, memory) of V2X cooperative perception, rather than chasing incremental accuracy. The motivation (Fig. 1) and framing around three bottlenecks (local inference, transmission, fusion) are clear and well-argued.

The work is a coherent full-stack system contribution: it unifies model-side post-training quantization (encoder, fusion, head) with a communication-side codebook-based message representation, and the paper shows these compose into an end-to-end quantized pipeline. This is a valuable engineering contribution for the community.

The alignment module (heterogeneity KL loss + spatial L2 loss) is a sensible and empirically effective remedy for the specific failure mode of naive quantization at the fusion stage. Fig. 3, Fig. 4, and Table 2 provide reasonably direct evidence that the alignment terms (not just the quantization) drive recovery from 97.4% to 99.8% and robustness under pose noise.

Experimental evaluation is broad and well-organized: three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), multiple fusion methods (Pyramid Fusion, F-Cooper, AttFuse, V2X-ViT, Who2com, Where2comm), heterogeneous agent configurations (LP+CR, LP+LS), and a clear split between model-level and system-level protocols.

Ablations are thorough (calibration data size, calibration steps, codebook size n_C and n_R, comparison to FP16 low-precision training, PD-Quant, LiDAR-PTQ) and reported in the appendix, which strengthens reproducibility. Power/throughput measurements and a real-world testing platform (V2X-RealO) add practical credibility.

The paper is well-written, figures are informative, and limitations (V2X-ViT degradation under aggressive quantization) and broader impact are discussed honestly. Code and an extended HEAL codebase are promised.
weaknesses: Novelty of the communication component is limited. The codebook-based message representation and code-index transmission closely mirror CodeFilling (Hu et al., 2024), which is cited and used as a baseline; the incremental contribution is mainly the coupling of this scheme with PTQ. The codebook learning (nearest-neighbor assignment + reconstruction loss) is essentially standard product-quantization / VQ-VAE style training.

The headline quantitative claim is potentially misleading. The abstract and introduction emphasize '+9.5 improvement in mAP30 over full-precision baselines,' but this is a system-level (latency-aware) number: in Table 3 the raw accuracy of QuantV2X (52.6/42.2) is actually slightly *below* the Upper-bound (53.8/43.5), and the full-precision baseline is heavily degraded only because of the imposed transmission-latency model. The actual perception accuracy is 'preserved' (~99.8% of FP), not improved. The improvement depends strongly on the specific latency simulation parameters (27 Mbps, uniform async delay up to 200 ms), which are borrowed from prior work but not stress-tested for sensitivity. The paper should foreground the accuracy-preservation result and present the latency-gain as the source of the system-level improvement.

'Fully quantized' is somewhat overstated: the system uses INT4 weights / INT8 activations (and INT8/INT8 for system-level), not sub-8-bit. The appendix argues 2-bit is impractical and unsupported by TensorRT, which is reasonable, but the terminology invites scrutiny.

The alignment module, while effective, is theoretically shallow. The KL and L2 losses are introduced without much analysis of why they specifically correct heterogeneity-induced activation-range shift and spatial misalignment, nor how the calibration objective in Algorithm 1 interacts with them. There is no comparison to simpler alternatives (e.g., per-agent activation calibration, or existing cross-agent normalization schemes).

Comparisons are incomplete in places. Quantization-aware training (QAT) is not evaluated even though the paper frames PTQ vs QAT as a trade-off; a QAT reference point would clarify how much accuracy is left on the table. System-level experiments only use PointPillar backbones, so the claim of general scalability across architectures is supported mainly at the model level.

Latency measurements are performed on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 (desktop GPU) with custom CUDA kernels, which weakens the 'in-vehicle / resource-constrained edge' narrative; true edge-device (e.g., Jetson Orin) numbers would be more convincing for the deployment claim.

The improvement in Table 1 at 4/8 bits is modest for some fusion methods (e.g., V2X-ViT drops from 57.4 to 29.9), and the paper acknowledges but does not resolve this; the practical applicability of the method therefore appears architecture-dependent.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem—deployment efficiency of V2X cooperative perception—with a coherent full-stack quantization pipeline that unifies model-side and communication-side efficiency.

Evaluation is unusually broad and system-oriented: model-level results on DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real and OPV2V, plus real-hardware system-level latency (ROS/TensorRT, RTX 3090), power/energy measurements, and a scaling study under GPU memory budgets.

The alignment module ablation (Table 2, Figs. 3–4) shows clear and consistent gains, especially under increasing pose noise, where the vanilla quantization baseline degrades sharply while the proposed method remains close to full precision.

Generalization is demonstrated across a range of fusion methods (Table 1) and against other PTQ baselines (Table 8), and the method outperforms LiDAR-PTQ on DAIR-V2X, supporting the applicability of the recipe.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: training/calibration settings (HEAL repo, 0.5% calibration data, 5,000 steps) and hardware/toolchain details are given, and the authors commit to releasing code.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the three pillars are largely adaptations—standard PTQ, a codebook message representation that closely follows CodeFilling (Hu et al., 2024), and 'alignment' losses that are essentially feature-level (KL) and output-level (L2) knowledge distillation from the full-precision model. The paper's claim of a 'novel alignment module' overstates the originality.

The headline claim of '+9.5 mAP30 improvement over full-precision' is derived from a latency-adjusted evaluation rather than raw detection accuracy. In raw accuracy QuantV2X is comparable to (and slightly below) full precision (e.g., Table 3 upper-bound 53.8/43.5 vs. 52.6/42.2), so the framing risks overstating the scientific contribution.

The latency-aware evaluation hinges on an arbitrary communication model (fixed 27 Mbps, asynchronous delay U(0,200) ms) and the mapping from latency to mAP is not clearly specified in the main text. Because the full-precision baseline drops ~10 mAP30 relative to the 'upper-bound' purely due to latency, the reported gains depend heavily on these modeling choices.

No quantization-aware training (QAT) baseline is included, even though the paper explicitly acknowledges that QAT is generally more accurate. A fair comparison under matched training/calibration budgets is missing, so it is unclear whether PTQ is the right design choice or simply a convenient one.

The codebook contribution is not isolated from CodeFilling (Hu et al., 2024); the incremental value of 'quantization-aware codebook learning' over prior codebook-based communication is neither clearly articulated nor quantified.
In Table 2 the alignment module only partially closes the gap to full precision in some settings (e.g., LP+CR: 74.0/66.4 vs. 75.1/68.2), indicating residual degradation that is not fully discussed.

The system-level experiments report INT8/INT8, while the more aggressive INT4/INT8 configuration is used mainly at the model level; the practical deployability of the INT4 configuration—central to the 'fully quantized' claim—is not fully substantiated at the system level.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: system-level efficiency (latency, bandwidth, memory) of V2X cooperative perception, rather than purely chasing accuracy metrics.

Proposes a unified end-to-end quantization strategy spanning encoder, fusion module, and detection head, together with a codebook-based low-bit message representation for inter-agent communication, which jointly targets computation and transmission bottlenecks.

Introduces two well-motivated domain-specific losses at the fusion stage (heterogeneity alignment via KL divergence and spatial alignment via L2 on bounding boxes) that materially reduce false positives and improve localization under quantization noise, as evidenced in Tables 2 and 10.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V) and, importantly, real-world deployment on the ROS-based V2X-RealLO platform with latency, power, and throughput measurements.

Generalization of the PTQ procedure is demonstrated across several fusion paradigms (Pyramid Fusion, F-Cooper, AttFuse, Where2Comm, Who2com), and ablation studies cover calibration size/steps, codebook size, and alignment components.

Provides a clean system-level latency decomposition into local inference, communication, and fusion latency, and quantifies the effect of each optimization (Fig. 5, Fig. 6), which strengthens the practical claims.
Reproducibility is supported by planned code release, use of public datasets/benchmarks, TensorRT deployment details, and explicit calibration/ablation recipes.
Discussion of limitations (2-bit infeasibility, degradation on V2X-ViT), broader impact, and LLM usage is included and appropriate.
weaknesses: The abstract's headline claim of '+9.5 mAP30 improvement over full-precision baselines' is misleading: this gain stems entirely from latency-induced degradation of the full-precision baseline under system-level evaluation, not from any intrinsic accuracy advantage. Compared to the ideal upper-bound, QuantV2X (52.6/42.2) is still below full precision (53.8/43.5).

Technical novelty is moderate: the core PTQ pipeline (block-wise reconstruction, AdaRound-style learnable rounding, max-min calibration, codebook quantization) heavily adapts existing methods (BRECQ, PD-Quant, AdaRound, CodeFilling). The contribution is largely a domain-integration effort rather than a fundamentally new quantization algorithm.

Generalizability is limited: Table 1 shows V2X-ViT collapses from 57.4/49.5 (FP32) to 40.0/11.0 under 8/8 quantization, which the paper acknowledges but does not resolve. This weakens the 'fully quantized' generality claim and suggests the alignment module does not adequately handle complex attention-based pipelines.

The codebook-based communication is conceptually close to CodeFilling [13] and Where2Comm [12]; the incremental gain over CodeFilling (52.6 vs 51.4 mAP30) is modest and mostly attributable to reduced latency rather than to better message representation.

The alignment module's design choices (KL divergence on fused BEV features, L2 on bounding boxes) are reasonable but somewhat ad hoc; no theoretical justification or analysis of why these specific losses address quantization-induced misalignment is given.

Some system-level comparisons rely on simulated communication latency (uniform U(0,200) ms) rather than measured wireless transmission, which may not fully reflect real deployment behavior; the real-world V2X-RealLO evaluation (Table 12) is smaller in scope.
Results depend on implementation details of TensorRT and custom CUDA kernels; failure modes or edge cases of the deployment (e.g., varying GPU architectures, thermal throttling) are not explored.

Latency speedups (3.2×) and accuracy preservation (99.8%) figures are reported from a specific configuration; sensitivity of these numbers to backbone, bit-width, and calibration data selection could be better characterized in the main text rather than deferred to the appendix.

strengths: Addresses a critical and practical gap in V2X cooperative perception: system-level latency, bandwidth, memory, and real-world deployability, not just detection accuracy.
Proposes a coherent full-stack quantization system combining PTQ, codebook-based message transmission, and a tailored alignment module for heterogeneous multi-agent fusion.
Extensive experiments on DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, and OPV2V, with multiple fusion methods, ablation studies, power consumption, scaling behavior, and real-world ROS-based deployment evaluation.
Demonstrates strong system-level results: 3.2× latency reduction and improved deployment-oriented mAP over full-precision baselines, with accuracy close to ideal upper-bound.
Good reproducibility details, clear architecture and calibration description, and a stated plan to open-source code and integration with V2X-ReaLO.
Motivation is compelling and clearly illustrated through latency decomposition and qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: The alignment module uses KL divergence between deterministic feature maps, but the distributions for the KL term are not formally defined; clarity on normalization or softmax treatment is needed.

The 'fully quantized' claim could be made more precise: codebook entries and certain deployment components may not be end-to-end quantized to low-bit formats, and exact bit-widths for all modules should be explicitly stated.
Quantization gains are weaker for attention-based fusion methods such as V2X-ViT, indicating limited generalizability to some modern architectures without further adaptation.
The paper is primarily empirical and systems-oriented; theoretical grounding for the alignment losses and codebook quantization is relatively light.
An explicit limitations section is absent, although appendix discussions partly compensate; a concise limitations statement would strengthen the paper.
System-level latency simulation relies on a simple uniform random delay model, which may not fully capture real-world communication variability.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: system-level efficiency, latency, and bandwidth in V2X cooperative perception, rather than only accuracy.
Provides a full-stack quantization pipeline spanning model inference and transmitted messages, with extensive experiments on DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, and OPV2V.
Evaluates on a real-world ROS-based V2X testbed (V2X-RealO) and reports latency, power, and scaling behavior under GPU memory constraints.
Includes ablation studies on calibration data size, calibration steps, codebook size, quantization bit-width, and alignment losses.
The proposed codebook-based message representation meaningfully reduces communication volume and is compared against relevant communication-efficient baselines such as Where2Comm and CodeFilling.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is incremental: the paper combines existing post-training quantization, codebook/VQ-style message compression, and feature-distillation-like alignment losses, without introducing a fundamentally new vision or learning algorithm.

The 'first fully quantized multi-agent system' claim is overstated; prior work already explores quantization for 3D detection and codebook-based communication for V2X, and the paper does not convincingly establish that end-to-end quantization of this pipeline has not been considered.

The alignment module is essentially knowledge distillation from a full-precision teacher (KL on fused features and L2 on boxes), but there is no comparison to standard distillation baselines, so it is unclear how much the proposed module contributes beyond teacher forcing during calibration.

System-level latency results rely on simulated communication delays rather than measured V2X network traces; the main paper does not sufficiently justify the latency model (f_s/v + U(0,200)) or show that the reported 3.2x speedup generalizes to real deployment conditions.

The quantization settings are inconsistent between model-level and system-level experiments (INT4/INT8 vs. INT8/INT8), and the full system is not evaluated under the same aggressive bit-width reported in the abstract's strongest claims.

Codebook synchronization and deployment are not adequately addressed: the codebook entries themselves are not quantized, and it is unclear how all agents maintain a shared, versioned codebook in real-time dynamic scenarios.

The paper is overlong and repetitive, with many key details deferred to the appendix; several claims, such as '+9.5 mAP30 over full-precision baselines,' depend heavily on the chosen baseline and simulated latency assumptions.
Comparisons to recent quantization methods for cooperative perception are limited, and the gains over CodeFilling in system-level accuracy are marginal while both use the same message size (0.03 MB).
